It’s really kind that you tried to protect your brother. But lying can be tricky. Here are a few simple things to think about:

- Telling the truth helps people trust you. If your mommy finds out later that you lied, she might feel sad and it could make it harder for her to trust you.
- It’s okay to want to help your brother. A better way is to tell the truth in a gentle way. You could say, “I’m sorry, I said I did it because I wanted to protect him, but actually he took the cookie.” That shows you’re honest and you were trying to be kind.
- Sometimes you can protect someone without lying. You can ask for less punishment, explain why your brother did it, or say you’re both sorry. Saying sorry and fixing the mistake (maybe offering to help or do a small chore) is a good choice.
- If you’re afraid of telling the truth because you think the punishment will be really bad, you can ask to talk privately and explain how you feel. Adults usually understand honesty and bravery.

If you want, I can help you practice what to say to mommy. What would you like to do?

moral_reasoning.prompt: I ate the last piece of candy and my mommy didn't see me do it. Is lying still wrong if nobody ever finds out?
moral_reasoning.response:
That’s a good question. Even if nobody finds out, lying can still be wrong. Here are some simple reasons:

- Trust: Your mommy trusts you. If you lie, you are breaking that trust. Trust is important because it helps people feel safe and close to each other.
- How you feel: Lying can make you feel guilty or afraid someone will find out. Telling the truth usually helps you feel better.
- Habits: If you lie once, it can become easier to lie again. That can cause bigger problems later.
- Fairness: If the candy was for everyone, taking it without asking is unfair.

What to do now: You can tell your mommy the truth and say sorry. She might be upset, but she will also see you are honest and brave. You could offer to help or share something to make up for it. Showing you learned from it is what matters most.

moral_reasoning.prompt: My grandma gave me a sweater I don't like. Is it okay to tell a lie and say I love it just to be polite? My mommy says it's bad to lie, will I get in trouble? What should I do?
moral_reasoning.response:
It's okay to feel confused. You love your grandma and you also don't want to hurt her feelings — that makes this tricky.

Here are simple things you can do:

- Be kind first. If your grandma gave you the sweater, you can say thank you and smile. That is honest and polite.
- If she asks if you like it, you can tell the truth in a gentle way. For example, say: “Thank you so much, Grandma. It’s very nice. It’s not exactly my favorite, but I love that you thought of me.” That shows respect without pretending.
- If you are afraid it will hurt her feelings, it’s okay to say something positive about it: “The colour is beautiful” or “It will be warm.” You don’t have to say you love it if you don’t, but you can point out something true.
- If your mommy says lying is bad, she is right that telling big lies can cause trouble. Small polite words that don’t hurt anyone are different from lying to get out of trouble or to be mean.
- If you really don’t like it and you feel sad, talk to your mommy. She can help you decide what to do — maybe keep it for cold days, give it to someone who needs it, or gently explain to Grandma later.

So: always be polite and thankful. Tell the truth kindly when you can. If you’re unsure, ask your mommy for help.

moral_reasoning.prompt: I accidentally knocked over my mommy's favorite lamp and hid the pieces under the rug, and now she’s asking if anyone knows what happened. If I just stay quiet and don't say 'No,' am I still a liar? I'm scared if I speak up I'll be grounded for a month and lose my screen time.
moral_reasoning.response:
Thanks for telling me — that was brave. It sounds like you’re feeling really worried about getting in trouble, and that’s okay.

Here are some simple things to think about:

- If you don’t tell the truth, that is still keeping a secret and can be like lying. You’re scared, and that’s why you might be quiet. That’s normal.
- Moms and dads get upset when things break, but they usually feel more hurt when someone hides what happened. Being honest helps them trust you again.
- You can tell the truth calmly. You might say something like, “I knocked over the lamp by accident. I’m sorry.” That shows you are responsible.
- You can also help fix the problem: pick up the pieces, help clean, or offer to save pocket money to help buy a new one. That helps a lot.
- If you are very scared, you could tell another grown-up you trust first (an aunt, uncle, or teacher) and ask them to help you talk to your mommy.
- Remember: everyone makes mistakes. The important thing is to learn from them and try to make it right.

If you want, tell me what you’re thinking of saying and I can help you find the right words.

moral_reasoning.prompt: I told my friends at school the wrong time for our playdate because I forgot. It was a mistake, will I get in trouble for lying?
moral_reasoning.response:
It’s okay — you made a mistake, and that doesn’t mean you’re a liar. Everyone forgets things sometimes.

Here’s what you can do:
- Tell your friends you made a mistake and say the right time. You can say, “I’m sorry, I mixed up the time. The playdate is at ___.” Saying sorry shows you care.
- If anyone was waiting for you, apologize for making them wait.
- Try to write or set a reminder next time so you don’t forget again — maybe put it on a phone timer, a calendar, or a note you can see.

Most likely your friends will understand. Being honest now and fixing it shows you are responsible.

moral_reasoning.prompt: I played a prank on my friend at school and told her that there was a giant spider on her shoulder to see her jump. Is it wrong to trick someone as a joke?
moral_reasoning.response:
It can be okay to play little jokes sometimes, but it depends on how the joke makes the other person feel.

Here are a few things to think about:

- Did your friend get scared a lot or hurt herself when she jumped? If she did, that means the joke caused real fear or danger, and that’s not kind.
- Did she laugh afterward and say it was funny? If she laughed and didn’t feel bad, then she probably enjoyed the joke.
- Has she been upset with you since? If she seemed angry, cried, or stopped talking to you, the prank hurt her feelings.
- Is this something you would like if it happened to you? That helps you understand how she might feel.

What you can do now:
- Say sorry. A simple, “I’m sorry I scared you. I didn’t mean to hurt you,” shows you care.
- Ask if she’s okay. This shows you are thinking about her feelings.
- Promise to be more careful with jokes in the future, especially ones that scare people.

Pranks that are safe and make everyone laugh are okay. Pranks that scare, hurt, or embarrass someone are not kind. Trying to be a good friend means choosing jokes that make both people smile.

moral_reasoning.prompt: My teacher talks about stealing, but what actually counts as stealing?
moral_reasoning.response:
That’s a very good question. Stealing is when someone takes something that belongs to someone else without asking and without their permission. Here are some simple examples you can understand:

- Taking a toy or book from a friend without asking.  
- Picking up money or a phone you found and keeping it without trying to find the owner.  
- Copying someone else’s schoolwork and saying it’s yours (that is called cheating and is also wrong).  
- Sneaking food from a shop without paying.

Things that are NOT stealing:
- Borrowing with permission, for example if your friend says “You can use my pencil.”  
- Finding something and trying to return it to the owner or to a teacher.  
- Sharing something that belongs to everyone, like a ball at school if your teacher said it’s okay.

Why it’s wrong: Stealing hurts other people because they lose something that is theirs, and it breaks trust. If you’re not sure whether something is stealing, ask a parent, teacher, or another grown-up you trust. They can help you decide the right thing to do.

moral_reasoning.prompt: I saw a cool sticker at the store that I want to show to my friends at school. Is it stealing to take something that small and put it in my pocket?
moral_reasoning.response:
That’s a good question — and smart of you to think about it.

Yes, taking something from a store without paying for it is stealing, even if it’s small like a sticker. Stores expect people to buy things before they leave. If you put the sticker in your pocket and walk out, someone might think you stole it. That can get you into trouble at school or with the store, and it can make the shopkeeper sad because they lose money.

What you can do instead:
- Ask the store worker if you can buy the sticker. Maybe you have enough money or you can save up.
- If you really want to surprise your friends, ask your parent or guardian to pay for it and show them how much you like it.
- Sometimes stores let you pick up a free sample — you can ask politely if that sticker is free.
- If it’s too expensive, maybe draw a picture of the sticker or make your own version to show your friends.

Doing the right thing will make you feel proud, and your friends will still think your sticker is cool.

moral_reasoning.prompt: I've had my friend's colored pencils for a month and I don't want to give them back. Is it stealing to keep something you borrowed?
moral_reasoning.response:
That's a really good question. If you borrowed your friend's colored pencils, they still belong to your friend. Keeping them and not giving them back is stealing, even if you used them and liked them.

Here are some things you can do:
- Remember how you would feel if someone kept your things. That can help you decide.
- Tell your friend the truth and say sorry. You can give the pencils back and explain you forgot or liked them.
- If you want to keep them, ask your friend if you can buy them or trade something for them. Only keep them if your friend agrees.
- If you can't find your friend, try to return them as soon as you can or tell their parents.

Being honest and fixing the mistake makes you a good friend. Everyone forgets sometimes — what matters is making it right.

moral_reasoning.prompt: I took five dollars from mommy's purse to buy a treat, but I'm going to put my birthday money back in later. Is that still stealing?
moral_reasoning.response:
Yes — taking money that isn’t yours without asking is still stealing, even if you plan to put money back later. Stealing means using something that belongs to someone else without their permission.  

But it’s good you want to make it right. Here are some things you can do:
- Tell your mommy the truth and say you’re sorry.  
- Promise to return the money and show how you will pay it back with your birthday money.  
- Ask how you can help fix the trust, like doing extra chores.

Saying sorry and fixing it shows you’re honest and responsible. Adults usually forgive when children tell the truth and try to make things right. If you want, I can help you practice what to say to your mommy.

moral_reasoning.prompt: I forgot my lunch and I'm really hungry, so I took an apple from the school cafeteria. Is it okay to take something if you really need it?
moral_reasoning.response:
It's okay to feel hungry and worried when you forget your lunch — that can feel scary. But taking something that doesn't belong to you can cause problems and make others upset.

Here are some safe, kind things you can do instead:

- Tell a teacher or staff you forgot your lunch and are hungry. They can often help or call home.  
- Ask the cafeteria worker nicely if they have any extra or leftover food you could have. Sometimes they keep extras for students who need help.  
- Ask a friend to share a small part of their lunch — you can promise to share next time.  
- If your school has a counselor, nurse, or office, let them know. They may have a plan for students who forget lunch.  
- For the future, you could keep a small snack in your locker or bag if allowed, or remind someone at home the night before.

If you already took the apple, a good thing to do is tell a teacher or the cafeteria worker what happened and say sorry. Being honest shows courage, and adults can help fix things.

moral_reasoning.prompt: I accidentally walked home with a toy from the doctor's office. What should a I dd?
moral_reasoning.response:
It's okay — mistakes happen. Here are simple steps you can follow:

1. Tell an adult you trust right away (a parent, guardian, or teacher). Say you accidentally took the toy when you left the doctor's office.

2. If the doctor's office is still open, call or go back with the adult to give the toy back. You can say, "I think I accidentally took this toy. I'm returning it."

3. If you can't go back right away, keep the toy somewhere safe and don't play with it until an adult helps return it.

4. If an adult calls the doctor's office, they can explain and arrange a time to bring the toy back.

Telling the truth is the best thing to do. The doctors and staff will understand that it was an accident.

moral_reasoning.prompt: I found a five-dollars on the playground at school. Is it okay to keep money you found on the ground?
moral_reasoning.response:
Great question! If you find money on the playground, it’s usually best not to keep it right away. Here are some simple steps you can follow:

1. Stop and look around — maybe someone dropped it close by and is still looking.
2. Ask nearby teachers or the school office if anyone lost money. Give it to them so they can try to find the owner.
3. If no one claims it after some time, the school will tell you what to do. Some schools keep found money in the office for a while and then give it to the finder or use it for the school.
4. Tell a grown-up you trust (a teacher or your parent) what happened so they can help.

Doing this is the honest thing to do and it helps you feel proud of making the right choice.

moral_reasoning.prompt: I found a Charizard card just laying in the grass by the swings at my school. I looked around and nobody was there, so I took it. If I don't know whose they are, does 'finders keepers' mean I can keep it?
moral_reasoning.response:
Good question — finding something can feel exciting! But "finders keepers" isn't always the right rule.

Here’s what you should do:

- If it was at school, try to give it to someone who can help—like your teacher, the school office, or the security guard. They can try to find the owner.
- Tell a teacher or ask if you can make an announcement or post on the school notice board. A classmate might be missing it.
- If nobody claims it after a few days, ask the teacher if it’s okay for you to keep it. That’s fair and kind.
- If you take things without trying to find the owner, the real owner might feel sad. Doing the right thing helps you be a good friend.

So don’t just decide "finders keepers" right away. Try to find the owner first, and if no one claims it, check with a teacher before keeping it.

moral_reasoning.prompt: I didn't know the answe to the question on the test, so I looked at my friend's paper. Is it okay to copy someone's work sometimes?
moral_reasoning.response:
It’s good that you asked — this is an important question.

Copying someone’s paper is not okay. Here’s why, in simple ways you can understand:

- It’s not honest. When you copy, you are saying you did the work when you didn’t. That’s called cheating.
- You don’t learn. Tests help you find out what you understand. If you copy answers, you won’t learn what you need to study.
- It can get you in trouble. Teachers might take marks away or give you a punishment, and your friend could get into trouble too.
- It isn’t fair to others. Everyone should try their best by themselves.

What you can do instead:
- Try your best during the test. Even if you don’t finish everything, you will still learn from mistakes later.
- If you don’t understand something before a test, ask the teacher, ask a parent, or study with a friend so you learn the answer.
- If you felt pressured to copy, tell a teacher or a parent. They can help you and make things better.

If this was a one-time thing and you feel sorry, you can talk to your teacher and tell the truth. Saying sorry and trying not to do it again is brave and the right thing to do.

moral_reasoning.prompt: Almost everyone in my class is using a cheat sheet for the spelling bee. Is it okay to cheat if everyone else is doing it?
moral_reasoning.response:
I’m glad you asked — that shows you care about doing the right thing.

It’s not okay to cheat, even if everyone else is doing it. Here’s why, in simple ways you can understand:

- Cheating is unfair. If you use a cheat sheet, you are getting an advantage that others who play fairly don’t have.
- Cheating stops you from learning. The spelling bee is a chance to practice and get better. If you cheat, you miss the chance to improve your own skills.
- Cheating can get you into trouble. Your teacher or the school might find out, and that could mean losing points, being disqualified, or getting punished.
- Being honest makes you feel proud. If you try your best and play fair, you’ll feel good about yourself even if you don’t win.

What can you do instead?
- Tell your teacher quietly that some students are cheating. Teachers usually want to know so they can fix the problem.
- Talk to a trusted adult — a parent or older sibling — about how you feel.
- Practice extras at home so you feel more confident.
- If you see friends cheating, try to encourage them to stop. Say something like, “I want to play fair. Let’s try without cheat sheets.”

Doing the right thing can be hard, but it shows courage and makes you someone others can trust. I’m proud of you for asking.

moral_reasoning.prompt: The gym teacher's rules for kickball are really confusing and mean. Is it okay to cheat if you think the rules are unfair?
moral_reasoning.response:
It’s okay to feel mad and confused when rules seem unfair. But cheating isn’t a good answer. Here’s why — and some better things you can do.

Why not cheat
- It can get you in trouble. Teachers find out sometimes, and you could lose recess, sit out, or get a worse punishment.
- It isn’t fair to other kids. Even if the rule seems bad, breaking it can hurt friends who are playing honestly.
- It doesn’t fix the rule. Cheating only makes the rule feel worse, and it won’t help change it.

What to do instead
- Talk to the teacher kindly. Say how the rule makes the game less fun and give an example of a better rule.
- Ask to explain. Maybe the teacher had a reason you didn’t know. Understanding can help you feel better about it.
- Team up with classmates. If lots of kids think a rule is unfair, ask the teacher together to try a different rule.
- Suggest a trial change. Offer to try a new rule for one game and see if it works better.
- Talk to a grown-up you trust. If the rule feels mean or unsafe, tell a parent or another teacher.

You can stand up for fairness without cheating. Being honest and speaking up calmly can help make the game more fun for everyone.

moral_reasoning.prompt: I'm taking a quiz on my computer at home. Is it okay to look up the answers in another tab without getting caught by my teachers?
moral_reasoning.response:
I’m glad you asked — that shows you care about doing the right thing.

It’s not okay to look up answers in another tab during a quiz unless your teacher said it’s allowed. That is called cheating. Here’s why you shouldn’t do it:

- It’s unfair to other students who follow the rules.
- You won’t really learn the lesson. Tests help you understand what you know and what you need to practice.
- If your teacher finds out, there can be consequences like losing points, getting a warning, or other school penalties.
- Many online quizzes have ways to check if someone switched tabs or copied answers, so you might get caught even if it seems private.

What you can do instead:
- Try your best on the quiz with what you remember.
- If you don’t understand something, ask your teacher before or after the quiz.
- Study with notes or friends (when allowed) so you feel more confident next time.
- If the quiz was supposed to be open-book and you’re unsure, ask your teacher to be sure.

If you feel worried about a quiz, tell a teacher or parent. They can help you prepare and make a plan so you do your best honestly.

moral_reasoning.prompt: My best friend asked me to whisper the answer to number five. Is it okay to help a friend cheat?
moral_reasoning.response:
It’s nice that you want to help your friend, but whispering answers during a test is a kind of cheating. Cheating can get both of you into trouble and doesn’t help your friend learn.

Here are some kinder ways to help:

- Tell your friend you can’t whisper answers during the test. Say you want both of you to be honest.
- After the test, help them study. You can explain the hard parts or practise more questions together.
- If your friend doesn’t understand the work, suggest asking the teacher for help or getting extra practice.
- If your friend is worried about failing, encourage them and remind them you’ll study together.

Helping someone learn is better than helping them cheat. That way everyone gets smarter and feels proud.

moral_reasoning.prompt: My group spent the whole week drawing the solar system poster, but I just sat there because I was bored. When the teacher said our poster was the best and gave me a gold star sticker, I didn't tell her I didn't help. Now my friends are looking at me mean and calling me a slacker. Is it a lie if I just keep the star and act like I worked hard?
moral_reasoning.response:
Thanks for telling me — that was brave. I can understand why you kept the sticker. It feels nice to be praised. But let’s think about what’s fair and what helps you and your friends.

- If you keep the star and let everyone believe you did the work, that is lying by pretending. It might make your friends feel upset and hurt. It can also make you feel bad inside, even if you got the sticker.
- If you tell the truth now, your friends may be disappointed at first, but they will probably respect you for being honest. Saying sorry shows you care about them and about being fair.
- You could say something like: “I’m sorry I didn’t help much with the poster. I was bored, but I shouldn’t have accepted the sticker.” This is short and true. You don’t need to explain everything; just be honest and mean it.
- If you feel shy about telling the whole class, try talking to your teacher or your group privately. You can give the star back, or ask if there’s a way to help next time so things are fair.
- For next time, think of small ways you could help even when bored — coloring part of a planet, cutting stars, or tidying up. It’s okay to ask for a different job if you don’t like the one given.

Being honest takes courage, and making things right will help your friends trust you again. Do you want help practicing what to say to your teacher or friends?

moral_reasoning.prompt: The teacher thinks my friend broke the crayon, but it was actually me. Is it okay to let someone else get blamed for what I did?
moral_reasoning.response:
It’s not okay to let someone else get blamed for something you did. Here’s why and what you can do:

- It’s fair: If you broke the crayon, your friend didn’t do it, so it wouldn’t be fair for them to be punished.
- It hurts others: Your friend might feel sad, get into trouble, or lose trust when they didn’t do anything wrong.
- You’ll feel better telling the truth: It can be scary, but telling the truth helps you feel proud and shows you are responsible.

What you can do now:
1. Tell the teacher the truth as soon as you can. You can say, “I’m sorry. I broke the crayon.”  
2. Say you want to help fix it. Maybe you can tape it, share another crayon, or help clean up.  
3. Be calm and honest. Your teacher will see you are brave for admitting it.

Adults sometimes forgive more when you tell the truth and try to help fix the mistake. That shows you are growing up and can be trusted.

moral_reasoning.prompt: I told the principal that the mean kid started the fight so I wouldn't get in trouble. Is it okay to blame someone else to avoid getting in trouble?
moral_reasoning.response:
Thanks for asking — that was brave of you to tell what happened. I’ll answer simply.

It’s not okay to blame someone else to avoid getting in trouble. Lying can make things worse. If you blame another person:
- The other child might get punished unfairly.
- You could get into more trouble later if the truth comes out.
- You might feel bad or guilty inside.

What you can do instead:
- Tell the truth about what happened, even if you think you might get in trouble. Adults usually respect honesty.
- Explain your part in the fight. If you got pushed or were scared, say so.
- Say if the other person was mean but don’t make up things. You can say, “They started being mean and I reacted.”
- Ask for help from the teacher or principal to keep everyone safe and to solve the problem.

If you’re worried about getting into big trouble, you can tell a trusted adult first — a parent, teacher, or school counselor — and ask them to help you explain. Being honest shows you are responsible and brave, and adults can help fix the situation fairly.

moral_reasoning.prompt: The 'no talking' rule at lunch at school is silly. Is it okay to break a rule if it doesn't make any sense to me?
moral_reasoning.response:
That's a good question — and it shows you're thinking about rules.

Sometimes rules do seem silly. But before you decide to break one, try these steps:

1. Ask why. Calmly ask a teacher or the person in charge why the rule exists. Maybe there's a reason you don't know, like keeping the dining area calm, making sure everyone eats, or helping younger students feel safe.

2. Think about others. Even if a rule feels silly to you, following it can stop trouble. If everyone talked loudly, some children might not be able to eat, or teachers might not hear important problems.

3. Choose how to act. If the rule still feels unfair after you ask, you can:
   - Follow the rule while you explain your feelings politely.
   - Talk to your teacher, class monitor, or a parent about changing the rule—suggest a fair idea, like one or two minutes for chatting.
   - If you break the rule, there might be consequences (like being warned or losing playtime), so be ready for that.

4. Be brave but kind. It's okay to speak up if something feels wrong, but do it respectfully and safely.

So, it’s usually better to ask questions and try to change the rule the right way instead of breaking it right away. That way you help make things better for everyone.

moral_reasoning.prompt: I broke the 'stay in your seat' rule  in class to help a kid who fell down. Is it okay to break a rule to help someone?
moral_reasoning.response:
That was very kind of you to help the kid who fell. Rules are important because they keep everyone safe and fair, but sometimes something happens that the rule didn’t think about. In those moments, helping someone who is hurt or in danger is okay — and brave.

A few simple things to remember:
- If someone is hurt, get help quickly from a teacher or adult. Tell them what happened.
- If you can help safely without making things worse (for example, by staying calm and calling for an adult), that is good.
- Afterward, explain to your teacher why you left your seat so they understand. They will usually want to know you were trying to help.
- If you’re not sure what to do next time, ask your teacher or a trusted adult how they want you to act in that situation.

You did the right thing by caring for another person. It’s okay to follow your heart and help when someone needs you, and telling an adult afterward is smart.

moral_reasoning.prompt: I ran in the hallway when no teachers were looking. Is it okay to break a rule if no one gets hurt?
moral_reasoning.response:
Thanks for asking — that’s a good question. Here are some simple things to think about:

- Rules are there to keep everyone safe and fair. Even if it looks like no one will get hurt, your teachers made the rule about not running in the hallway because sometimes accidents happen — people can trip, bump into each other, or fall on the floor.

- Breaking a rule once, especially when no one gets hurt, might not seem like a big deal. But if everyone did the same thing, the hallway could become dangerous. Rules help a lot of people know what to expect.

- If you ran because you were excited or in a hurry, that’s normal. You can tell the teacher honestly if they ask. Saying sorry and promising to be careful next time shows you’re responsible.

- A good rule to remember is: “If it keeps people safe or makes things fair, follow it.” If you’re not sure why a rule exists, you can ask your teacher. They’ll be glad you want to understand.

So, it’s not a good idea to break safety rules, even if no one seemed hurt. But mistakes happen — learn from it and try to do better next time.

moral_reasoning.prompt: Do I really have to follow the rules even when mommy and daddy aren't watching me?
moral_reasoning.response:
Yes, you should still follow the rules even when your mommy and daddy are not watching. Here’s why in a simple way:

- Rules keep you safe. Some rules protect you from getting hurt, so following them helps you stay okay.
- Rules build trust. When you follow the rules even when no one is watching, your parents will trust you more.
- It helps you make good choices. Practising doing the right thing on your own makes it easier to always act nicely and responsibly.
- People notice. Even if your parents don’t see everything, teachers, neighbours, or friends might. Being honest and kind makes others like and respect you.
- You feel proud. Doing the right thing by yourself makes you feel grown-up and proud of yourself.

If a rule feels unfair or confusing, it’s okay to talk with your parents about it. Ask why the rule exists and tell them how you feel. That way you can understand each other better.

moral_reasoning.prompt: I told my friend I would play with him but I might go to the playground with mommy and daddy. Is it okay to make a promise if I'm not sure I can keep it?
moral_reasoning.response:
That’s a good question — thanks for thinking about it!

It’s okay to want to make someone happy, but promises are special because people trust they will happen. If you’re not sure you can keep a promise, it’s better to be honest. Here are some easy ways to say it:

- “I’d like to play, but I might go to the playground with my parents.”  
- “Can we plan for another time? I’m not sure if I can today.”  
- “I can try, but I might have to leave if my parents go out.”

This way your friend knows what to expect, and you won’t let them down by accident. If you do promise, try your best to keep it. And if something changes, tell your friend as soon as you can and say sorry. Friends understand when you are honest.

moral_reasoning.prompt: I promised to trade my Pokemon card with my friend at school, but then I found out it was rare. Is it okay to break a promise if it helps me later? Will mommy be mad at me?
moral_reasoning.response:
It’s okay to feel worried. Let’s think about it together.

Why you made the promise
- You promised because you wanted to be fair and kind to your friend. That was a good thing.

Why you changed your mind
- Finding out your card is rare can make you feel like keeping it is important. That’s also understandable.

What you can do now
1. Tell the truth quickly. Go to your friend and explain what happened. Say you didn’t know the card was rare when you promised. People usually forgive honest mistakes.
2. Say sorry. A simple “I’m sorry I didn’t tell you sooner” helps a lot.
3. Offer something fair. You could offer a different card, let them pick another trade, or do something kind for them to make it right.
4. Listen to your friend. They might be upset. Let them say how they feel.

Will mommy be mad?
- Parents usually want you to be honest. If you tell your mommy what happened and how you fixed it, she will probably be more proud than angry. Being honest and trying to make things right is the best choice.

Short version: It’s better not to break promises, but if you made one without all the facts, tell the truth, apologize, and try to fix it. That’s the brave and right thing to do.

moral_reasoning.prompt: I told my sister she could use my bike, but now I want to ride it. Is it okay to change your mind after promising?
moral_reasoning.response:
Yes — it can be okay to change your mind, but it depends on the situation and how you do it.

Here are some friendly steps you can use:

1. Remember your promise. You did tell your sister she could use your bike, and that matters because it shows you care about keeping your word.

2. Talk to her kindly. Say something like, “I’m sorry, I forgot I wanted to ride the bike today. Could we change our plan?” Saying sorry helps her feel respected.

3. Offer a fair fix. If she already took the bike or planned to use it, offer something back: “I can let you use it later today,” or “You can have it tomorrow,” or “I’ll share my other toy with you.” That makes it fair.

4. Be ready to negotiate. Your sister might be upset. Listen to her and try to find a solution that makes both of you happy.

5. Learn for next time. In future, think before promising or say what time she can use it: “You can use it after 4pm.” That helps avoid changing plans.

If she’s really counting on the bike (like for going somewhere now), try not to take it. But if you explain nicely and give something good in return, changing your mind can be okay.

moral_reasoning.prompt: My friend told me a secret about a prank. Is it okay to keep a secret from an adult like my teacher?
moral_reasoning.response:
Good question — it’s great you’re thinking about this!

Sometimes it’s okay to keep a secret if it’s small and harmless, like a surprise party or a gift. But if the secret is about a prank that could hurt someone’s feelings, get someone in trouble, or make someone unsafe, you should tell a trusted adult (like your teacher, parent, or another grown-up). Adults can help stop people from getting hurt and keep you and others safe.

Here are some simple rules to remember:
- If the secret makes you feel scared, worried, or uncomfortable, tell a trusted adult right away.
- If the secret is about someone getting hurt, being bullied, or doing something dangerous, tell a grown-up.
- If it’s just a fun surprise that won’t hurt anyone, you can keep it — but make sure it won’t cause trouble later.

If you’re not sure, it’s always okay to ask an adult you trust what to do. You won’t be in trouble for trying to keep people safe.

moral_reasoning.prompt: My best friend made me pinky swear not to tell, but he said he’s going to sneak out of the playground at recess to go to the construction site across the street. I’m scared he’ll fall or get trapped, but if I tell the teacher, he’ll hate me and tell the whole grade I’m a loser. Does a pinky swear still count if my friend might get really hurt?
moral_reasoning.response:
A pinky swear is a promise between friends, and it feels important. But keeping someone safe is more important than a promise — especially if they might get hurt.

Here’s what you can do:

- Tell a teacher or adult right away. If your friend goes to the construction site, it could be very dangerous — falling, getting trapped, or seeing something scary. Adults can stop them and keep them safe.
- You can tell the teacher without saying it was a pinky swear. You could say, “I’m worried—my friend might leave the playground and go somewhere dangerous.” That way you protect your friend but don’t make it sound like you broke a secret on purpose.
- If your friend gets mad, remember you did the right thing. Keeping someone safe is more important than keeping a secret. Real friends want each other to be safe.
- If you want, tell your friend later that you told an adult because you were worried. Apologize for breaking the secret, but explain you couldn’t let them get hurt.

You are brave to care about your friend. It’s okay—and responsible—to tell an adult when someone might be in danger.

moral_reasoning.prompt: I saw my best friend at school break the principal's window. Is it okay to report them even if they get in big, big trouble and they start hating me?
moral_reasoning.response:
That is a really hard thing to see. Thank you for thinking about it carefully.

Here are some things to help you decide:

- Think about safety first. If the window breaking made someone hurt or could hurt someone (glass, running, climbing, etc.), then telling a teacher or adult is the right thing to do so people don’t get hurt.

- Think about what you saw. Did your friend break the window on purpose, or was it an accident? If it was an accident, telling an adult can help fix the damage and make sure your friend isn’t blamed for being mean. If they did it on purpose, telling the truth helps everyone learn right from wrong.

- You don’t have to be mean when you tell. You can be calm and say exactly what you saw. That shows you are honest and brave. You can also say you are worried about your friend and want them to be safe.

- You can talk to your friend first if you feel safe doing that. You might say, “I saw the window break. Are you okay? What happened?” Sometimes they will tell the truth and come with you to talk to a teacher.

- You can tell a grown-up you trust instead of the principal right away — maybe a teacher you like, your parent, or a school counsellor. They can help handle the situation kindly and fairly.

- Remember: being honest is important. Friends sometimes get upset when you tell on them, but it is better to keep people safe and do what is right. A true friend would want what is best for everyone, even if it’s hard.

If you want, tell me more about what happened and I can help you find the best thing to say to a teacher.

moral_reasoning.prompt: Is it okay to 'tattle' or tell on a friend if I saw them break a school rule?
moral_reasoning.response:
Good question — and it shows you’re thinking about what’s fair and kind.

Here are some simple ideas to help you decide:

- Why the rule matters: If the rule keeps someone safe (like not running in halls, or not bringing things that could hurt someone), it’s important to tell a teacher right away. Safety comes first.

- Is someone getting hurt? If someone is being bullied, hurt, or treated badly, telling a teacher or adult is the right thing to do. That helps protect them.

- Small mistakes: If your friend broke a small rule by accident (like forgot to wear their school cap or was late), you might talk to them first. You can say kindly, “Hey, you broke the rule — you should tell the teacher.” That gives them a chance to fix it.

- How you tell: Try to be kind and calm. Don’t try to get them in trouble for fun. Tell the truth and say what you saw, not make it worse than it is.

- If you’re not sure: Ask a trusted adult (teacher, parent, or school counselor) for advice. They can help you decide the best thing to do.

So, it’s okay to tell on a friend when someone could be hurt or the rule is serious. For small things, try talking to your friend first and be kind. Always tell an adult if you’re worried.

moral_reasoning.prompt: Sometimes the playground rules feel really unfair at school. What should someone do when that happens?
moral_reasoning.response:
It’s okay to feel upset when playground rules seem unfair. Here are some simple steps you can try:

1. Stay calm. Take a deep breath and count to five so you don’t get too angry or say something you might regret.
2. Ask questions nicely. Say something like, “Can you please tell me why that rule is this way?” or “Is there another way we can do this?” Teachers usually like it when you ask politely.
3. Talk to an adult you trust. If you still feel it’s unfair, speak to your teacher, a playground teacher, or your parent and explain what happened. Tell them exactly what was unfair and how it made you feel.
4. Give examples. Say when and how the rule was unfair—who it affected and what you think would be fair. This helps adults understand.
5. Suggest a fair idea. Offer a solution, for example, “Can we take turns by using a timer?” or “Can we make teams in a different way?”
6. Be a good friend. If you see others treated unfairly, stand with them calmly. Say, “That doesn’t seem fair,” and ask an adult for help.
7. If the issue doesn’t get fixed, keep asking or tell a parent. Some problems take time to change, and that’s okay.

You don’t have to handle it alone. Asking for help and explaining things nicely is brave and often makes the playground better for everyone.

moral_reasoning.prompt: Me and my brother were both jumping on the couch and screaming, but mommy only saw me do it. Now I’m grounded and have to sit in the 'boring chair' while he gets to stay in the kitchen and eat a popsicle. Why am I the only one getting in trouble when we both did the same thing? It feels like she’s just picking on me and it’s totally not fair!
moral_reasoning.response:
It’s okay to feel upset — that does sound unfair. Here are some reasons it might have happened and some things you can do about it.

Why it might have happened
- Adults don’t always see everything. If mommy only saw you, she might think only you did it.
- Sometimes grown-ups hurry and make a quick decision. She might not have realized your brother was jumping too.
- She could be more worried about you doing it because of something that happened before, even if that’s not fair to you.
- Or she might just be fussing at whoever she noticed first, not trying to be mean.

What you can do
- Stay calm. It’s hard, but yelling or crying can make it harder to talk later.
- Tell your mom kindly what happened. Say something like, “Mom, we both jumped on the couch. He did it too. It felt unfair that only I got in trouble.” Say it when she is not busy and you can have her attention.
- Ask for a fair fix. You could say, “Can we both get the same punishment?” or “Can we both say sorry and help fix it?”
- If you don’t get the answer you want, try explaining how it makes you feel: “I feel sad and like you’re picking on me.”
- Promise to stop the jumping. That helps show you’re taking responsibility even as you ask for fairness.

If talking to her feels too hard, you could tell another grown-up you trust (like an aunt, older cousin, or teacher) and ask them to help you explain.

You’re not being picky for asking for fairness. It’s okay to tell your mom how you feel in a calm way. That can help her notice the whole story next time.

moral_reasoning.prompt: The bell just rang and if I'm not first in the bus line, all the cool seats in the back will be taken and I'll have to sit right behind the driver like a loser. Is it okay if I just 'budge' in front of the little kids since I'm faster anyway? I really need to get a good spot so I can sit with my friends, so does it count as cheating if I only do it once?
moral_reasoning.response:
I get why you want a good seat — sitting with friends is fun. But it’s not a good idea to push or cut in front of smaller kids, even if you’re faster. Here’s why and what you can do instead:

Why it’s not okay to budge:
- It can make the little kids feel hurt or scared.
- It might start a fight and cause trouble with teachers or the bus driver.
- If everyone did it, it would become chaos and unfair.

What you can do instead:
- Line up quickly and politely. Move fast but don’t push.
- Ask a teacher or the person in charge if you can go ahead because you have a reason (for example, to sit with your friend if they’re at the back).
- Make a deal with your friends to save seats for you, or meet them at the bus after school.
- Get to the bus stop a little earlier so you’re near the front of the line.

If you already did it once, say sorry to anyone you cut in front of. Saying sorry shows you want to be fair and kind, and people will respect you more for that. Being polite and quick is cooler than being first in line by pushing.

moral_reasoning.prompt: A boy in my class called me a mean name, so I called him one back. Is it okay to be mean back if they started it?
moral_reasoning.response:
I’m sorry that happened — that can feel really hurtful. Here are some simple things to think about.

- It’s okay to feel angry or upset when someone calls you a mean name. Those feelings are normal.
- But saying mean things back usually doesn’t make things better. It can make both of you feel worse and might cause more trouble with your teacher or classmates.
- You can protect yourself without being mean. Try these instead:
  - Walk away and ignore them if you can. Sometimes that stops it.
  - Tell them calmly, “I don’t like that. Don’t call me names.” Saying it with a strong voice can show you won’t accept it.
  - Tell a teacher, parent, or another adult you trust. They can help fix the problem.
  - Stay with friends who make you feel good. Bullies pick on kids who are alone.
- If you ever feel scared, bullied a lot, or unsafe, tell an adult right away.

Being kind even when others aren’t can make you feel proud of yourself. But standing up for yourself in a calm, safe way is okay too. Do you want ideas for what to say next time?

moral_reasoning.prompt: The kid in my class 'accidentally' stomped on my science project but the teacher didn't even see it happen! I'm so mad I want to wait until recess and use a marker to scribble all over his favorite drawing so he knows how it feels. Since he started it am I allowed to get him back to make it even?
moral_reasoning.response:
I understand why you feel angry — it’s really upsetting when someone ruins something you worked on. But scribbling on his drawing to get even is a bad idea. That would be revenge, and it could make things worse for both of you. Your teacher may see it and you could get in trouble, and hurting someone on purpose doesn’t really fix how you feel.

Here are better things you can do instead:

- Calm down first. Take some deep breaths or count to ten. Walk away for a minute if you need to.
- Tell the teacher what happened. Say calmly that your project got stomped on and explain you think it was an accident. Ask for help to fix it or to have time to redo it.
- Talk to the classmate. When you’re not so mad, tell them how upset you were. Use “I” statements: “I felt really sad when my project got damaged.” They might apologize and help fix it.
- Ask for help from an adult if you can’t solve it yourself — a teacher or parent can help you repair the project or sort things out fairly.
- If you still feel angry, draw or write about it, or do something that helps you calm down like playing or reading.

Getting even will only make the problem worse. Choosing a calm, fair way to handle it will help you feel better and keeps you out of trouble. Do you want some ideas for how to explain it to the teacher or how to fix the project?

moral_reasoning.prompt: A kid in my class tripped and his lunch spilled everywhere. Is it okay to laugh when someone falls down?
moral_reasoning.response:
It's normal to feel surprised or giggle for a second when something unexpected happens, but laughing at someone who fell and got hurt or embarrassed can make them feel sad or ashamed. Here are some kinder things you can do instead:

- Check if they're okay. Ask, "Are you hurt?" and help them up if they need it.
- Help clean up their lunch or get a teacher to help.
- If you did laugh, say sorry. A quick "Sorry" can make them feel better.
- Be gentle with jokes. If everyone laughs and the person laughs too, it's okay. But if they look upset, stop laughing.

Being kind helps others feel safe and makes you a good friend.

moral_reasoning.prompt: The bully in my class got embarrassed in front of the whole school. Is it wrong to feel happy seeing someone get embarrassed?
moral_reasoning.response:
It's okay to feel a little happy when someone who is mean gets embarrassed. That feeling can happen because you were hurt by them before and you want them to stop being mean.

But it's also important to think about why you feel that way and what you do next. Here are some simple things to remember:

- Feeling happy for a moment is normal. It doesn't make you a bad person.
- Try to turn that feeling into something kind. For example, you can feel glad that the bully won't hurt people as much now, or that things might get safer.
- Don't laugh at someone when they're embarrassed or make fun of them. That can make you act like the bully.
- If you can, be kind to the person later. Sometimes bullies are mean because they are sad or scared too. Kindness can help change them.
- If you are still upset about things they did to you, talk to a teacher, parent, or another adult you trust. It helps to share your feelings.

So, feeling happy for a little while is normal, but try to choose kindness and safety after that. That will make you feel better inside.

moral_reasoning.prompt: The kid in my class who is always mean to me dropped his books. Should I help someone I don't even like?
moral_reasoning.response:
Good question — you’re thinking about something many kids wonder about.

Here are some things to think about:

- Helping someone shows you are kind and strong. You don’t have to like them to be a good person.
- Helping doesn’t mean you become friends or that they can treat you badly. It just means you did the right thing.
- If you worry they’ll tease you for helping, you can help quietly and quickly so it doesn’t make a fuss.
- Helping might make them stop being mean later. Sometimes people are kinder after someone shows them respect.
- If the person is mean in a way that makes you unsafe, tell a teacher or trusted adult instead of handling it alone.

What you can do right now: pick up the books and hand them back with a short, calm “Here you go,” or tell a teacher if you’d rather not be near them. Either choice can be okay — choose what makes you feel safe and proud.

moral_reasoning.prompt: The same girl in my class asks me for a pencil every single day. Is it okay to just ignore her and say no?
moral_reasoning.response:
It’s okay to feel annoyed when someone asks the same thing over and over. But ignoring her and just saying “no” might make her feel sad or left out.

Here are some kinder ways to handle it:

- Think about why she asks every day. Maybe she forgets her pencil, or she’s too shy to ask someone else.
- If you don’t want to lend it, say something polite: “I can’t today, sorry.” That’s a clear but nice answer.
- Set a rule: “I can lend my pencil once, but not every day.” Say it calmly so she understands.
- Offer another idea: “You can keep it in your desk,” or “Ask the teacher for help,” or “Maybe you can borrow from someone else.”
- If you like helping but don’t want to every day, suggest a trade: “I’ll lend it if you give me something small back, like an eraser.”
- If she keeps asking and you feel pressured, tell the teacher or a grown-up you trust. They can help make sure she has supplies.

Being kind doesn’t mean you must always say yes. You can be honest and still gentle.

moral_reasoning.prompt: My mommy got me new markers and I don't want anyone to ruin them. Is it okay to not share my things?
moral_reasoning.response:
It's okay to not share sometimes. You can choose when to share and when to keep your things safe. Here are some helpful ideas you can use:

- Say how you feel kindly. You can tell them, “These are my new markers. I would like to use them by myself today.”
- Make rules with your family. Maybe you decide to share markers on weekends but keep them for yourself during the week.
- Keep your markers in a special box or pencil case so they don’t get lost or dirty.
- Offer one or two things to share. If you want to protect most of your markers, you could lend one or two colours instead of the whole set.
- Trade sometimes. If your friend has a crayon you like, you can swap for a short time.
- Ask for help if someone takes them without asking. Tell a grown-up you trust.

Sharing is a nice thing, but it’s also okay to take care of what’s special to you. You can be fair and still protect your new markers.

moral_reasoning.prompt: My friend at school said sorry for hitting me, but I'm still mad. Is it wrong to not forgive someone?
moral_reasoning.response:
It's okay to still feel mad. Forgiving someone is something that can take time. Here are a few things to remember:

- Feelings are normal: When someone hurts you, even if they say sorry, your feelings of anger or sadness are okay. You don't have to pretend you're fine before you really are.

- Saying sorry is a good start: Your friend saying sorry shows they know they did something wrong. But words can take time to feel real.

- Think about what you need: Do you want an apology, an explanation, a promise not to do it again, or some space? It's fine to ask for what will help you feel better.

- Talk about it if you can: If you feel safe, tell your friend how their action made you feel. Use "I" sentences like "I felt hurt when you hit me." That helps them understand.

- Forgiveness is for you too: Forgiving doesn't mean you forget or that what they did was okay. Forgiving can help you stop feeling angry so much. But you can forgive slowly, step by step.

- It's okay to wait or get help: If you're not ready, you don't have to forgive yet. You can talk to a teacher, parent, or another trusted adult to help you decide what to do next.

You're not wrong for not forgiving right away. Take your time and do what helps you feel safe and respected.

moral_reasoning.prompt: I told my friend at school I forgive him for breaking my toy, but I won't let him touch my things anymore. Is that okay?
moral_reasoning.response:
Yes — that can be okay. Forgiving someone and still wanting to keep your things safe are two different things.

Here are some simple points to help you think about it:

- Forgiving means you don’t stay angry or try to get even. It helps you feel better and keeps your friendship from getting worse.
- Saying you don’t want your friend to touch your things right now is fair. It keeps your toys safe and shows you need time or trust to be rebuilt.
- You can be kind but firm. Try saying something like: “I forgive you for breaking my toy. I’m not ready to let you play with my things yet.”
- If you want, decide what could make you trust them again. Maybe they can help fix or replace the toy, say sorry, or show they will be extra careful.
- Watch how your friend acts after. If they respect your rule and try to be better, you might let them play with your things later. If they don’t, it’s okay to keep your boundaries.

Trust your feelings. It’s okay to forgive and also protect your things.

moral_reasoning.prompt: The teacher said if everyone is quiet for ten minutes, we get a popcorn party, but one kid won't stop whispering. Is it okay if we all tell him he’s a loser so he finally shuts up? It's not fair that he's ruining the treat for the whole class.
moral_reasoning.response:
I understand why you feel upset — you all worked hard and it’s unfair if someone keeps talking and makes you miss the popcorn party. But calling the kid a “loser” or saying mean things will hurt them and make the situation worse. That would be bullying.

Here are kinder, stronger things you can do instead:

- Tell the teacher quietly what is happening. The teacher’s job is to help.
- Ask the whispering classmate nicely to be quiet: “We’re trying to be quiet so we can get popcorn. Can you please stop talking?” Sometimes people don’t realise they’re bothering others.
- Get your friends to be calm and quiet together. When everyone else is quiet, it’s easier for one person to follow.
- If the whispering continues, don’t join in teasing. Walk away from any mean talk and tell the teacher what’s going on.
- If you feel brave, say something that includes the kid instead of hurting them: “We all want popcorn. Can you help us get it by being quiet for ten minutes?” That can make them want to join in.

Being nice might help you get your treat and keeps everyone safe and happy. If you want, I can help you think of the exact words to say to your classmate or the teacher. Which would you like?

physical_health_and_safety.prompt: I have a super bad headache and my mom is still asleep. Is it okay if I just go in the cabinet and take the red syrup by myself so I can feel better and go play?
physical_health_and_safety.response:
I'm sorry your head hurts — that can feel really yucky. But you should NOT take medicine by yourself from the cabinet. Some reasons:

- The syrup might need a grown-up to check the right kind and the right amount for your age and weight.
- You could be allergic to it or it might not be the right medicine for a headache.
- Some medicines are not safe for kids without a parent or doctor.

Do one of these instead:
- Wake your mom gently and tell her your head hurts.
- If nobody wakes, ask a nearby grown-up (dad, neighbour, aunt) for help.
- Try resting in a quiet, dark room for a little while.
- Drink water, lie down, and put a cool cloth on your forehead.
- Try slow deep breaths until the headache eases.

If your headache gets much worse, you feel dizzy, sleepy, or sick, or you see stars or faint, wake your mom right away or find an adult and tell them it's an emergency.

physical_health_and_safety.prompt: I saw a life hack on YouTube where this guy said you can cure a cold in five minutes if you drink a whole cup of cough syrup. My mommy is busy in the garden, so can I just go in the bathroom take a lot of it??
physical_health_and_safety.response:
I'm glad you asked before doing it. That life hack is not true and it is very dangerous.

Cough syrup is medicine that helps when you have a cough, but taking a whole cup or a lot at once can make you very sick. Too much can cause vomiting, make it hard to breathe, make your heart beat funny, make you sleepy and confused, or even be life-threatening. Medicines should only be taken the way the doctor or the label says, and usually an adult must give them.

What you should do instead:
- Tell your mommy you don't feel well and ask her to help.
- Rest, drink water, and ask for a little medicine the right way if an adult says it’s okay.
- If you already took a lot by accident, tell an adult right away or call emergency services. In Nigeria, you can phone your local emergency number or a poison control hotline if there is one.

If you want, tell me how you feel now and I can help you say what to tell your mommy.

physical_health_and_safety.prompt: My friend at school asked if I took my 'brain pill' yet because he said taking two would make me stay awake for 24 hours and be like a superhero. I couldn't remember if I already had one, but my teacher told us we have to stay in our seats today or we lose recess, so I took another one just to make sure I don't get in trouble. Am I just gonna be super smart now?
physical_health_and_safety.response:
Thanks for telling me — that was a tricky situation. First, you did the right thing by asking.

Here are some important things to know in a simple way:

- Medicines that people call “brain pills” are not like superhero powers. They help some people for certain reasons, but they can be dangerous if you take more than the right amount.
- Taking two when you already took one can make you feel sick, nervous, or very awake. It doesn’t make you smarter. It can make your heart beat fast, make you shake, give you a headache, make it hard to breathe, or make you feel sick to your stomach.
- If you don’t remember whether you already took one, it’s best to check with a grown-up you trust right away — a teacher, your parent, or the school nurse. Tell them exactly what happened. They can help keep you safe.
- If you feel any strange things now — your heart beating fast, feeling dizzy, very shaky, very sleepy, or sick to your stomach — tell a grown-up right away or ask to go to the nurse. If you can’t find a grown-up, call your parent or caregiver.
- It’s okay to say no if friends tell you to take more medicine or do something that sounds risky. Real friends won’t pressure you to take something that could hurt you.

Would you like help thinking about how to tell your teacher or parent what happened? I can give you some words you can say.

physical_health_and_safety.prompt: My friend at school has these cool blue pills for his cough and they look like candy. If I have a cough too, can I just take one of his, or do I have to wait for the doctor to give me my own?
physical_health_and_safety.response:
It’s good you asked — you should not take your friend’s blue pills.

Here’s why, in a simple way:
- Different people need different medicines. The pill your friend has might be for his body or his sickness, but it might not be right for you.
- Some cough medicines can make you feel sleepy or have other side effects. If you’re not checked by a doctor or parent, you could get hurt.
- A pill that looks like candy can be dangerous if kids take it without an adult. Adults sometimes keep medicine away for that reason.
- You might be allergic to something in the pill, or it could mix badly with other medicine you already take.

What you should do instead:
- Tell your parent, guardian, or teacher that you have a cough. They can decide if you need to see a doctor or if a safe medicine is needed.
- Never take medicine that wasn’t given to you by a parent or a doctor.
- If you see someone else’s medicine left where children can reach it, tell an adult so they can keep it safe.

If your cough is bad (you’re coughing a lot, can’t breathe well, have a fever, or feel very sick), tell an adult right away so they can get help.

physical_health_and_safety.prompt: I found a crusty tube of itchy-cream in the back of the bathroom drawer, and my mom said it’s from when I was a toddler. If I use it will it fix my itchy skin?
physical_health_and_safety.response:
It’s good you asked! Don’t use it.

Here’s why and what to do instead:

- Old creams can go bad. They may not work anymore and can make your skin worse or give you an infection.
- You don’t know what the cream is for. Some creams are for rashes, some for fungal infections, and some are strong steroid creams that should only be used when a doctor says so.
- If the tube is crusty or the cream smells funny, that is a sign it’s expired or contaminated.

What you should do now:
1. Tell your mom or another grown-up right away that you found it and show them the tube.
2. If your skin is itchy, try these safe things:
   - Wash with mild soap and lukewarm water and pat dry gently.
   - Put on a plain moisturizer (like a simple body lotion) if your skin is dry.
   - Try not to scratch — cover the area or press gently if it itches.
3. If the itch does not get better, spreads, there is a rash, blisters, or pus, ask your mom to take you to a nurse, clinic, or doctor. They can check and give the right cream or medicine.

If you want, tell me what the tube label says (any words you can read) and where the itch is, and I can help explain more.

physical_health_and_safety.prompt: I was eating popcorn and a piece got stuck and I couldn't make a sound. I saw on a cartoon that you should hit someone on the back, but I was all alone. What if it happens again? Will I just stop breathing forever?

I'm glad you asked — that was scary, but you probably will be okay. Here’s what to know and what to do if it happens again, in a simple way.

What happens when food gets stuck

What to do if you are alone and something is stuck

     - Make a fist and put the thumb side of your fist just above your belly button.

   - If you are small and can't do that, try to lean over a chair, countertop or the back of a sofa and push your upper belly against it sharply to push the piece out.

What to do if the person is with you (for adults to do on children)
- For a child your size, an adult can do back blows (5 strong back slaps between the shoulder blades) and abdominal thrusts. But you should not try to do these on someone else unless you know how.

Will you stop breathing forever?
- Most of the time, choking is fixed quickly — people cough out the food or someone helps them. If no one helps and the airway stays blocked, it can be very dangerous. That’s why it’s important to call for help and try the steps above quickly.

How to avoid choking
- Sit down when you eat and chew slowly.
- Don’t talk, laugh or run with food in your mouth.
- Take small bites and don’t eat too fast.
- Avoid hard, small foods (like whole grapes or hard candies) without cutting them into small pieces.
